The four basic functions of management (Fayol, condensed) are planning, organizing, leading, and controlling.

• Planning – defining goals, establishing a strategy for achieving those goals, and developing plans to integrate and coordinate activities. Example: a store manager sets a goal of 10% sales growth and decides on a promotion campaign.
• Organizing – determining what tasks need to be done, who will do them, how tasks are grouped, who reports to whom, and where decisions are made (designing the structure).
• Leading – working with and through people to accomplish goals: motivating subordinates, directing their activities, selecting the most effective communication channels and resolving conflicts.
• Controlling – monitoring actual performance, comparing it with the goals that were set, and correcting any significant deviations.

The functions are not a strict sequence – managers do them continuously and simultaneously, and controlling feeds back into planning.

Studying management is important for three main reasons:

1. The universality of management – management is needed in all types and sizes of organizations, at all levels, in all work areas and in all countries. Everybody has a stake in seeing organizations well managed, because we interact with them every day.
2. The reality of work – after graduating, you will either manage or be managed. Even if you never become a manager, understanding how managers think and behave helps you work with your boss, your co-workers and the organization.
3. Rewards and challenges – being a manager offers the chance to create a work environment where people do their best, to make a difference, to get recognition, status and good pay; but it is also hard work with ambiguous situations and limited resources.

So studying management is useful for future managers and non-managers alike.

Customer satisfaction is increasingly important because:

• Without customers, organizations would not survive – customers are the reason organizations exist, and competition (often global and online) gives customers more choices than ever. Dissatisfied customers can switch easily.
• Economies have shifted toward services: in service work, the employee's interaction with the customer IS the product, so employee attitudes and behavior directly shape satisfaction.
• Social media and online reviews mean one bad experience can quickly reach thousands of potential customers, while loyal, satisfied customers spread positive word of mouth.
• Loyal customers are cheaper to keep than new ones are to win, and a loyal customer base helps well-managed companies prosper even in difficult economic times.

Therefore managers must create a customer-responsive organization where employees are friendly, courteous, knowledgeable and responsive to customer needs.

Creativity – the ability to combine ideas in a unique way or to make unusual associations – is important because it lets a decision maker appraise and understand a problem more fully, "see" problems others can't, and, most importantly, identify all viable alternatives (step 4 of the decision process). Without creativity, managers tend to pick from obvious, conventional options and may miss the best solution, especially for unstructured problems.

Example: 3M's Art Fry had a weak glue that nobody could use. When he noticed paper bookmarks falling out of his choir hymnal, he combined the two ideas and created Post-it Notes. Another example: a restaurant facing long lines introduces online ordering with pickup lockers instead of simply hiring more cashiers.

Creativity can be stimulated by expertise, creative-thinking skills and intrinsic motivation, and by an environment with time, resources and little pressure or surveillance.

Electronic meetings combine the nominal group technique with computer technology: members sit at terminals (or join online), questions are presented, and members type their responses, which are displayed anonymously to everyone.

They help avoid groupthink because:
• Anonymity – people can give honest opinions without fear of disapproval or pressure to conform; dominant members or high-status people cannot silence others.
• Honesty – ideas are judged on their merits, not on who proposed them, which reduces minority domination.
• Speed and parallel input – everyone can "talk" at once without stepping on each other, so many more ideas are produced.

This enhances creativity because more alternatives are generated and unusual ideas are not filtered out. Drawbacks: the fastest typists can outshine others, and the lack of face-to-face communication loses some information and richness.

All three are standing plans for programmed decisions on structured problems, but they differ in how much discretion they leave.

• Procedure – a series of sequential steps used to respond to a structured problem. Example: the steps a purchasing department follows to order supplies: check inventory, fill out a purchase request, get approval, place the order.
• Rule – an explicit statement that tells a manager what can or cannot be done; no discretion. Example: "Employees must wear a hard hat in the production area" or "No refunds without a receipt."
• Policy – a guideline for making a decision; it sets general parameters and leaves room for interpretation and judgment. Examples: "We promote from within whenever possible" or "Customer satisfaction is our top priority." Terms like "whenever possible" or "satisfactory" signal the discretion involved.

In short: procedure = steps, rule = do/don't (most rigid), policy = guideline (most flexible).

1. Identifying a problem – recognizing a discrepancy between an existing and a desired state of affairs. Example: a sales manager notices that the department's laptops are so slow that sales reps lose time.
2. Identifying decision criteria – deciding what is relevant in making the decision. Example: price, weight, battery life, screen size, warranty.
3. Allocating weights to the criteria – prioritizing the criteria; the most important gets e.g. a 10 and others are weighted against it. Example: battery life 10, price 8, weight 6, warranty 4.
4. Developing alternatives – listing viable alternatives that could resolve the problem, without evaluating them yet. Example: listing five laptop models (Dell, HP, Lenovo, Apple, Acer).

The remaining steps are: analyzing alternatives, selecting an alternative, implementing it, and evaluating decision effectiveness.

All three are multinational corporations (MNCs), but they differ in where management and decision making sit:

• Multidomestic corporation – decentralizes management and other decisions to the local country; local employees run each country's operation and tailor products to the local market (e.g. Nestlé, Unilever, Frito-Lay).
• Global corporation – centralizes management and decisions in the home country; the world is treated as an integrated market and the home office controls foreign operations (e.g. Sony, Toyota, Deutsche Bank).
• Transnational (borderless) organization – eliminates artificial geographical barriers; there is no single home country and the structure is organized by business/industry groups instead of country (e.g. IBM dropping its country structure). Goal: efficiency and effectiveness in a competitive global marketplace.

Arguments FOR social responsibility: public expectations (society expects it); long-run profits (socially responsible firms tend to have more secure long-term profits); ethical obligation (it's the right thing to do); public image; better environment; discouraging further government regulation; balance of responsibility and power (businesses have a lot of power, so they should have matching responsibility); stockholder interests (it improves share price in the long run); possession of resources (business has the resources to help solve problems); superiority of prevention over cures (better to fix problems before they become expensive).

Arguments AGAINST: violation of profit maximization (business's only social responsibility is to make profits – classical view, Milton Friedman); dilution of purpose (distracts from the primary goal of economic productivity); costs (many social actions don't cover their costs and someone – often consumers via higher prices – must pay); too much power (business already has a lot of power); lack of skills (managers lack the skills to address social issues); lack of accountability (there are no direct lines of accountability for social actions).

Overall, most research finds a small positive relationship between social involvement and economic performance.

A strong culture is one in which the key values are intensely held and widely shared by employees; a weak culture is one where values are not clearly defined, held by only a few people, or not deeply committed to.

Effects on behavior:
• In a strong culture, culture has a much greater influence on employees' and managers' behavior: everyone knows "the way we do things around here", which creates consistency, loyalty and commitment, and lowers turnover. A strong culture can substitute for formal rules – fewer written rules and regulations are needed. It also guides how managers plan, organize, lead and control.
• The risk of a strong culture: it can resist change and stifle new ideas or diversity when the environment changes.
• In a weak culture, employees rely more on formal rules, procedures and direct supervision; behavior is less predictable and there is less shared commitment, but the organization may be more open to change.

Strong cultures are associated with high performance when the values fit the organization's strategy and environment.

Strategic plans apply to the entire organization and establish its overall goals; they are made mainly by top managers, usually cover a longer time frame (often 3+ years) and are broad. Example: "become the market leader in Asia by 2030."

Tactical (operational) plans specify how the overall goals are to be achieved: they are made mainly by middle and lower-level managers, cover a narrower part of the organization (a department or function), have a shorter time frame and are more detailed/specific. Example: the marketing department's quarterly ad campaign that supports the strategic goal.

The difference is breadth (strategic vs. tactical); both must be linked through a means-ends chain so that tactical plans serve as the means to reach strategic ends.

Management by objectives (MBO) is a process of setting mutually agreed-upon goals and using those goals to evaluate employee performance.

Key elements:
1. Goal specificity – goals are specific and measurable.
2. Participative decision making – managers and employees set goals jointly (not top-down only).
3. Explicit time period – each goal has a deadline.
4. Performance feedback – continuous feedback on progress toward goals.

Goals cascade through the organization, so individual goals support unit and organizational goals (means-ends chain).

Why it works: employees feel a sense of ownership of goals and are more motivated; studies show MBO can increase performance and productivity, especially with top-management commitment. Limitations: it is less effective in dynamic environments where goals constantly change, it can over-emphasize individual goals at the expense of teamwork, and it can become a paperwork exercise.

Creativity is the ability to combine ideas in a unique way or to make unusual associations between ideas. Innovation is the process of taking a creative idea and turning it into a useful product, service or method of operation. Creativity is the first step; innovation turns it into something of value.

The creative process has three steps: perception (seeing things from a unique perspective), incubation (ideas gel over time – sometimes years) and inspiration (the moment all prior efforts come together). Innovation then turns the inspiration into a useful product or process.

In the workplace, innovation is key to competing in a fast-changing ("white-water") environment – companies like 3M or Apple depend on a steady stream of new products. Managers stimulate creativity and innovation through the right structure (organic, flexible, plenty of resources, good communication), culture (accepting ambiguity, tolerating the impractical and mistakes, focusing on ends rather than means, low external controls) and human resource practices (training, job security, idea champions). Example: Art Fry's Post-it Notes at 3M.

Three sets of variables stimulate innovation:

1. Structural variables – organic structures (less formalization, centralization and specialization) make it easier to be flexible and share ideas; abundant resources allow managers to afford innovations and absorb failures; frequent inter-unit communication breaks down barriers; minimal time pressure and work/nonwork support (e.g. supportive supervisors) help creativity.

2. Cultural variables – an innovative culture accepts ambiguity, tolerates the impractical, has low external controls, tolerates risk and conflict, focuses on ends rather than means, has an open-system focus and provides positive feedback. Mistakes are treated as learning opportunities.

3. Human resource variables – the organization actively promotes training and development, offers high job security so employees aren't afraid of being fired for mistakes, and encourages people to become idea champions who actively and enthusiastically support new ideas, build support and overcome resistance.

External forces creating the need for change include:

• Changing consumer needs and wants – customers' tastes shift (e.g. demand for healthier food or online shopping), so companies must adapt products and services.
• New governmental laws and regulations – e.g. the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act forced employers and insurers to change their practices.
• Changing technology – new technologies (e.g. AI, smartphones, e-readers) can make existing products obsolete and require new processes (disruptive innovation).
• Economic changes – recessions, interest rates or a booming economy change demand, costs and strategy.

Example answer with two forces: (1) Technology – the rise of e-readers like Kindle forces libraries and publishers to change their services; (2) Government laws – new environmental or health-care regulations force companies to change processes and costs. Managers must monitor these forces and act as change agents to adapt the organization.

A matrix structure assigns specialists from different functional departments to work on one or more projects led by a project manager. It creates a dual chain of command: employees report both to their functional manager and to the project manager, so it violates the unity-of-command principle. When a project is finished, specialists return to their functional departments.

Advantages: fluid and flexible design that can respond to environmental changes; faster decision making; efficient use of specialists across projects; combines functional expertise with project/product focus; good for complex, multiple projects (e.g. aerospace, consulting).

Disadvantages: complexity of assigning people to projects; task and personality conflicts; confusion and power struggles because of two bosses; unclear accountability; employees can experience stress and ambiguity; requires strong communication and coordination.

A learning organization is an organization that has developed the capacity to continuously learn, adapt and change. Employees continually acquire and share new knowledge and are willing to apply that knowledge in making decisions or doing their work.

Structural aspects it needs:
• Boundaryless/flexible structure – minimal structural and physical boundaries so people can share information and collaborate across functions and levels.
• Teams – employees work in cross-functional teams on what needs to be done; empowered teams make decisions.
• Empowerment – managers act as facilitators, supporters and advocates rather than bosses.

Other characteristics: open information sharing (organizational learning can't take place without information), leadership that creates a shared vision that everyone agrees on, and a strong culture with a strong sense of community, caring and trust, where people feel free to openly communicate, experiment and make mistakes.
